core: Working definition of early adulthood: the developmental period spanning roughly the twenties and thirties, between adolescence and middle adulthood

Age-band slices: OpenStax Psychology 2e defines early adulthood as 19-29; OpenStax Lifespan Development treats 18-29 as the first phase of early adulthood; Erikson-based schemes map young adulthood to about ages 18-40; honest note: no single official timeline
Physical peak in early adulthood: muscle strength, lung function, and immune system functioning at their peak; people within early adulthood are typically at their healthiest
Health behaviors: choices made in young adulthood have immediate AND long-term health influences
Cognitive growth: thinking becomes more pragmatic and expertise deepens with experience as adult roles are taken on
Psychosocial tasks: Erikson's stage 6, intimacy versus isolation, associated with young adulthood; identity refinement continues
Levinson's life-structure theory: the overall pattern of roles (work, family, friendships) built in early adulthood
Honest framing: early adulthood as the engine room of the life course
supporting: Erikson's stage 6 age band (about 18-40) as cited by Simply Psychology
Work life development: exploring options, then committing to a line of work and building skill
The relationship between early adulthood and emerging adulthood (first phase)
The relationship between early adulthood and middle adulthood (generativity; onset of physical decline)
outOfScope: Detailed physical development topics (e.g., sexual health, fertility, specific disease epidemiology) — covered in depth by health/biology subjects
Intimacy and romantic relationships in depth — owned by the relationships topic
Emerging adulthood in depth (Arnett's five features) — owned by the emerging-adulthood topic
Middle adulthood in depth (generativity, midlife transitions) — owned by the middle-adulthood topic
Medical or clinical guidance of any kind

claims.claim: Early adulthood is the developmental period spanning roughly the twenties and thirties, between adolescence and middle adulthood; developmental texts slice the age band differently — OpenStax Psychology 2e defines early adulthood as ages 19-29, and the OpenStax Lifespan Development text treats 18-29 as the first phase of early adulthood.

During early adulthood many physical capabilities are at their peak, including muscle strength, lung function, and immune system functioning, and people within early adulthood are typically at their healthiest.
Choices made in young adulthood have immediate and long-term health influences: habits established in early adulthood — sleep, exercise, diet, care-seeking — shape health for decades.

Erikson's sixth psychosocial stage, intimacy versus isolation, is associated with young adulthood; its task is forming close, committed relationships, and failing to risk closeness can lead to isolation. Erikson-based reference schemes commonly map the stage to about ages 18-40.
The social and emotional themes of early adulthood center on intimacy, relationships, and work; identity refinement continues as earlier explorations consolidate into adult commitments.

Daniel Levinson's life-structure theory describes the overall pattern of a person's life at a given time — the arrangement of work, family, friendships, and other roles — and treats early adulthood as the period when the first adult life structure forms.

There is no single official timeline for early adulthood: texts slice the age band differently (19-29; 18-29 as a first phase; young adulthood through about forty) and people move through the period's tasks at very different paces.
Cognitive growth in early adulthood is marked by increasingly pragmatic thinking and by expertise that deepens with experience, built in the settings of work and relationships.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What age range defines early adulthood?
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e places early adulthood at ages 19-29 in its lifespan scheme.
OpenStax Lifespan Development treats 18-29 as the first phase of early adulthood (overlapping emerging adulthood), with chapter 11 covering physical and cognitive development in those years.
Simply Psychology's Erikson stages reference maps stage 6 (intimacy vs. isolation) to young adulthood, commonly cited as about ages 18-40.
The life-course view runs early adulthood through the thirties and early forties (settled careers, relationships, households).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the honest synthesis: early adulthood roughly spans the twenties and thirties, each scheme's slice is named explicitly, and no single official timeline is claimed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is early adulthood defined by the physical peak or by psychosocial tasks?
positions: The physical-peak account emphasizes muscle strength, lung function, immune functioning, and typical health at its best during early adulthood.
The psychosocial account (Erikson; the social/emotional chapter of the Lifespan Development text) emphasizes intimacy, work, and identity refinement as the defining tasks.
Popular framing treats early adulthood as 'the prime,' which can reduce the period to biology.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the physical peak as real but secondary: the period's defining tasks are psychosocial, and the physical peak matters largely because it makes habit effects easy to ignore.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does peak health make young adults' habits inconsequential?
positions: Because people in early adulthood are typically at their healthiest, the short-term consequences of poor habits are often invisible.
Choices made in young adulthood have immediate and long-term health influences, so habits established now matter for decades.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both facts together: peak functioning and long-term consequences are not in tension — the peak is exactly why 'fix it later' feels plausible, and the long-term influence is why it is a mistake.
